Container.Name: deadair
Container.Overview:
An AI radio station: it picks the records, writes what the presenter says between them, speaks it, and streams the result.
Everything is in this one container — the station, its console, the audio chain and the stream server. Pick the tag that matches what your server already runs:
deadair/deadair:latest — a voice is included; point it at your own PostgreSQL and Redis. deadair/deadair:full — brings its own database and cache as well. Nothing else needed. deadair/deadair:slim — no voice either; for pointing at a speech server on another machine.
Everything it keeps lives under one path, so backing it up is backing up one share.
First run: open the console on the WebUI port and sign in. The database schema is applied automatically. The stream is served by this same container at /live.mp3, so whatever you put in front of the WebUI port (a reverse proxy or a tunnel) carries the station too.
On Spotify there are TWO authorizations on the plugin page, and the station needs both. The connection lets the plugin read your library; the playback authorization below it lets the station fetch the audio. With only the first, your playlists list perfectly and nothing ever plays. The page Spotify sends your browser to will not load — that is expected, not a failure — so copy that address out of the bar and paste it back into the console.
Container.Requires: An x86-64 server: there is no arm64 image yet. On the latest and slim tags, a PostgreSQL database that already exists and a Redis server; the full tag brings both. On the slim tag, a speech server as well. Music comes from your own Spotify account or Subsonic server, such as Navidrome, because the station holds none of its own.
Container.DefaultTagDescription: A voice included. Bring your own PostgreSQL and Redis.

Branch.TagDescription: Brings its own database and cache as well. Nothing else needed.
No voice. For pointing the speech plugin at a speech server on another machine.

Config.Name: WebUI
Config.Description: The console, the API and the stream, all on this one port.

Config.Name: Data
Config.Description: What the station IS: its settings, presenters, schedule, pronunciations and ratings, installed plugins, the stream's own credentials, the audio you recorded yourself, logs — and, on the full tag, the database holding most of it. Small, authored, and the thing to back up. Belongs on the cache pool.

Config.Name: Media
Config.Description: Optional, and only about size. What the station HOLDS rather than what it is: records downloaded before they air, cover art, the speech it rendered, voice previews, the speech model's weights. All of it can be produced again by running the station, and it grows to roughly the size of the library you play — so put it on the array and leave it out of your backups. Blank keeps it under Data, which is fine until the library gets big.

Config.Name: Public address
Config.Description: The address a browser actually reaches this station at, including https:// — used to build sign-in redirects, so a wrong value here means a sign-in that lands nowhere.

Config.Name: Console address
Config.Description: Normally the same as the public address, because one port serves both.

Config.Name: Timezone
Config.Description: An IANA zone name such as America/New_York or Europe/London. The station reads the clock in this when it says the time and when it works out what half of the day it is; left unset a container reports UTC, which is a presenter saying "tonight" through your afternoon. Only the fallback — the station's own "Where the station is" setting, on the settings page, wins over it, because a station is a place and its listeners are in it rather than wherever the server happens to sit.

Config.Name: Secret key
Config.Description: Encrypts every credential the station stores, including your music provider's. Generate once with: openssl rand -hex 32 — it must be hex, and keep it. Losing it means entering all of them again.

Config.Name: Session key
Config.Description: Signs sessions, RS256, so it must be an RSA key. Generate one with: openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:2048 | base64 -w0 — a key is several lines and this field is one, so base64 it and paste that. Losing it signs everybody out and nothing worse.

Config.Name: Database host
Config.Description: Your PostgreSQL server. Leave every database and cache field blank on the full tag, which runs its own.

Config.Name: Database name
Config.Description: Must already exist; the station creates its own schema inside it, not the database itself.

Config.Name: Database user
Config.Description: Owns the schema: the station applies its migrations as this user at every start.

Config.Name: Runtime database user
Config.Description: Optional, and both this and the password below have to be filled in for either to take effect. A second, non-owner role for the request path, holding DML grants only, so a request cannot alter the schema — migrations still run as the owner above. Leave both empty to run everything as the owner, which is what happens today.

Config.Name: Cache host
Config.Description: Your Redis server. Sessions live here rather than in the database, so losing it signs everybody out and costs nothing else.

Config.Name: Sign-in client id
Config.Description: Optional, for signing in with Google. Without this the station signs you in with a one-time code instead. Register the public address followed by /api/auth/login/oidc/callback as the OAuth client's authorized redirect URI in the Google Cloud console.

Config.Name: Proxy in front
Config.Description: Leave empty unless a tunnel or a reverse proxy sits in front of this station. When one does, every listener reaches the station as THAT, so they all share one rate limit and the listener count collapses to however many different players are tuned in. Naming the proxy here — an address or a CIDR, and 172.16.0.0/12 covers another container on this box — lets the station see who actually asked. Only name something you put there yourself: it means believing an address that arrives in a header.

Config.Name: Proxy address header
Config.Description: Which header the proxy above puts the listener's address in. X-Forwarded-For suits almost everything; a Cloudflare tunnel also sends CF-Connecting-IP. Ignored while the field above is empty.

Config.Name: Apply migrations at start
Config.Description: Leave on unless you apply the schema yourself. An out-of-date schema otherwise degrades quietly rather than failing.
